title: The closed and the open saying: the power that joins, the square makif of bina, and the chashmal
overview:
Chapter 44 carries the division of the letters of thought up to its root. The sayings start as a *maamar stum*, a closed saying in hidden thought (*Elokim*, the 32 times "and G-d said" that open in *bina*), and become a *maamar psuach*, an open saying, in speech. The root of the power to divide is higher than *bina*. The text calls it *metzaref*, the power that joins. Thinking takes an idea apart, and speaking puts it back together, and real analysis takes the gun or the bridge apart only in order to rebuild it. Otherwise it is destruction.

*Bina* itself has two *mems*: the open part one already thinks in, and the closed, square *makif*, the part one does not yet understand, which sits on the head like a low ceiling. Understanding that has not set is flowing water. Once it is grasped it freezes into ice, the *rakia*, and the root of that ice is above *bina*: the *levush hachashmal*, which guards the *middos* and is the source of letters. A dog has feelings and even some *bina*, but without words it cannot feel an idea or ask "Why me?"

terms.gloss: a closed saying: the letters still hidden in thought; the sayings as they are in bina, and the part of bina one is still thinking about
an open saying: thought opened into divided letters, as in speech, and the part of bina one already thinks in
the closed (final) mem, square and shut on every side: the makifim of bina
the open mem, which has a mouth: closed thought opened by dividing it into letters
the power that joins; real analysis divides in order to put back together, so the text says metzaref where one expects mechalek
the power that divides, the work of thinking; it gets its strength from the power that joins
knowledge; it surrounds what it knows from every side and sits right on it
firmament; something fixed: comprehension once it has a set form
ice: an idea grasped in one particular way, which can no longer flow
flowing water: a deep idea not yet limited in the mind, which can still be understood in various ways
embodiment: putting an idea into an explanation, a mashal, letters
the garment of chashmal (chash, to feel, and mal, to speak): the letters, a guard over the middos, from above bina

sections.title: The closed saying and the open saying: Elokim and the 32 sayings that open in bina
sections.summary: The division of the letters of thought goes up through every level of thought to the *Atzmus*. "And *Elokim* said" starts there as a *maamar stum*, a closed saying in hidden thought, and becomes a *maamar psuach*, an open saying, in the speech of *Malchus*.

phrases.he: (מד) ומעתה יובן גם כן שרש ענין ההתחלקות דאותיות המחשבה מבחינת ה׳ גבורות מנצפ"ך כו',
ולמעלה מעלה גם במחשבה העצמית ומחשבה הקדומה ומחשבה סתימאה דאדם קדמון ואריך אנפין כו',
עד מחשבה דזעיר אנפין, על דרך הנזכר לעיל בפרטיות הענין באדם התחתון, ששרש התחלקות הצירופים באים מלמעלה ממקור ההשגה דבינה עצמה כו'
וזהו ענין מאמר סתום ומאמר פתוח
כמו ויאמר אלהי״ם, אלהי״ם ק"ך צירופים
phrases.en: you can put *Elokim* together 120 different ways

phrases.he: דמחשבה סתימאה שבעצמות ממש, נקרא מאמר סתום בעצמות סתימא דכל סתימין כו' עד רום המעלות, כמו אלהי״ם הבין דרכה כו'

blocks.text: The chapter applies what was said of a person below: the root of the division of letters comes from the source of comprehension of *bina* itself, at every level of thought up to the hidden thought of *Arich*. That is the *maamar stum* (closed saying) and the *maamar psuach* (open saying). *Elokim* has 120 combinations. *Vayomer Elokim*, "and G-d said", speaks of the *Elokim* in the *Atzmus* (the Essence): the saying that comes down from *Atzilus* to *Beriya* starts higher.

phrases.he: ובחינת אלהי״ם הזה הוא בחינת הצמצום וההסתלקות, וכמאר רבותינו זכרונם לברכה בתחלה עלה במחשבה לברוא במידת הדין שהוא שם אלהי״ם כו'
והיינו בחינת התחלקות צירופי אותיות שבמחשבה סתימאה גם כן
(כמו לפי תרגום אונקלוס בראשית בקדמין, שהוא הרצון הקדום היינו הרצון שבמחשבה הקדומה כו' נקרא בחינת אלהי״ם בבחינת הצמצום וההתחלקות
לפי מאמר רבותינו זכרונם לברכה דבראשית נמי מאמר הוא,
phrases.en: the *Bereishis* itself is also a *maamar*

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת מאמר סתום במחשבה הסתומה,
עד גם בבחינת מחשבה הפשוטה והעצמית כנזכר לעיל

blocks.text: This *Elokim* is *tzimtzum* (contraction) and withdrawal; that is what *Elokim* means. So the Sages say, "At first it arose in thought to create with the attribute of judgement," which is the Name *Elokim*. It is the division of the combinations of letters in the hidden thought as well. And by the saying that *Bereishis* too is a saying, **the *Bereishis* itself is also a *maamar***, a closed saying in the closed thought. The closed thought itself is really a *tzimtzum* of the simple thought of the Essence.

phrases.he: וכידוע דאלהי״ם אותיות מי אלה,
שהוא בחינת התחלקות
מי ברא אלה כו'
phrases.en: who created these

phrases.he: ואלהי״ם עלאה, בינה ומחשבה סתימאה דאריך אנפין ואדם קדמון כו', ואלהי״ם תתאה בחינת מלכות דתבונה ולאה וכו'
וכמו שכתוב בזוהר
דל"ב ויאמר אלהי״ם
phrases.en: it says *vayomer Elokim* 32 times

phrases.he: הן ל"ב שבילין דמתפתחין בבינה
שכולן בחינת מאמר סתום
phrases.en: all of these are in a way of a *maamar stum*

phrases.he: דדיבור שבמחשבה, שמזה נעשה מחשבה שבדיבור דמלכות
phrases.en: from the *dibur sheb'machshava* it becomes a *machshava sheb'dibur* of *Malchus*

phrases.he: שנקרא מאמר פתוח,
כמו שיתבאר בענין בחינת מ"ם סתומה ומ"ם פתוחה כו')
phrases.en: This will be explained more later.

blocks.text: *Elokim* is the letters *mi eleh*: division, *mi bara eleh*, **who created these**. The higher *Elokim* is *bina* and the hidden thought of *Arich Anpin*; the lower, *Malchus* of *tevuna* and *Leah*. The *Zohar*: **it says *vayomer Elokim* 32 times**, the 32 paths that open in *bina*. **All of these are in a way of a *maamar stum***, speech within thought, which becomes the open saying in the speech of *Malchus*.

sections.title: The root of division is above bina: the voice of bina, and the power that joins
sections.summary: The voice of *bina* is heard only in the division of letters in speech, and the power to divide comes from above *bina*. The text calls it *metzaref*, a joining: thinking takes an idea apart and speaking puts it together, but real analysis takes a thing apart only in order to put it back, or it is destruction.

phrases.he: ואמנם הנה שרש כח ההתחלקות הזאת, אף על פי שהוא בא בבחינת הצמצום,
הנה הוא מלמעלה מכח ומקור עצם ההשגה כו'
phrases.en: it really comes from higher than *bina*

phrases.he: וכמו שכתוב בזוהר על פסוק וקול התור נשמע בארצינו כו',
שהוא בחינת קול דבינה שנשמע בבחינת התחלקות צירופים
phrases.en: the voice of *bina* is not heard in the voice; it's heard in the division of the letters in the speech

phrases.he: על ידי בחינת ה׳ גבורות מנצפ"ך כו',
שהוא בבוא האור בבחינת הדבור, עלמא דאתגליא שנקרא ארצנו כו'
phrases.en: when the light of the *bina*, the light of the *sechel*, comes into revelation in the *dibur*, which is called *alma d'isgalya*

blocks.text: Until now he was setting up for a later explanation; now he gets to the actual point of the chapter. Although this division comes by way of *tzimtzum*, the root of the power to divide **really comes from higher than *bina***, higher than the power and source of comprehension itself.

The *Zohar* on "the voice of the turtledove is heard in our land": the voice of *Zeir Anpin* is heard in the voice itself, but the voice of *bina* is an inner voice that is not heard. It is **heard in the division of the letters in the speech**. So a dog's emotion can be heard, but it cannot bring the voice of *bina* into speech, which comes through dividing the letters by the five places of the mouth. This is **when the light of the *bina*, the light of the *sechel*, comes into revelation in the *dibur***, the revealed world, "our land."

phrases.he: וכנזכר לעיל באריכות ממשל התנוק
שאין לו מחשבה בהתחלקות אותיות כי אם כשידבר כו'
phrases.en: *davka* when he can speak, then his *machshava* can have *hischalkus osios*

phrases.he: דבזמן שיש מצרף לדבור מחכמה מבחינת פנימיות חכמה
phrases.en: *davka* when the *dibur* has a *metzaref*, a unification, from the *pnimiyus chachma*, from the *koach hamaskil*

phrases.he: אז יש מצרף לאותיות דמחשבה מפנימיות ומקור דבינה כו'

blocks.text: As explained at length with the *mashal* of the small child, who has no thought divided into letters until he speaks: ***davka* when he can speak, then his *machshava* can have *hischalkus osios***, division into letters. When speech has a *metzaref* (joining) from the inner *chachma*, from the *koach hamaskil* (the power that conceives), like the light of *mazal elyon*, then the letters of thought have a *metzaref* from the inner source of *bina*.

blocks.question: He says *tziruf* (joining) of the divisions of letters. Should he not say *chiluk*, division? The two are opposites.
blocks.text: They are opposites, but the division comes *davka* from the joining. That is how *bina* works: only when speech has its joining from *chachma*. Look at how you talk; talking is not like thinking. When you are just thinking, trying to figure something out, you keep looking at the *nekuda* (point) of *chachma*, but your main effort is to break it up, to analyze it into little pieces.

Talking is not like that, though it is hard to see: when you talk, you are putting it together. The analysis has to have been done already, or you could not talk. You cannot talk about something you never thought about, doing the analysis while you speak.

blocks.title: The absent-minded professor
blocks.text: When you are *mamash* (really) thinking deeply, in *iyun* (close analysis), you cannot talk. Try talking to the absent-minded professor: he can't. When he is really thinking his wife gets mad that he isn't talking to her, but it is because he is thinking.

Why? There is no *chachma* without *bina* and no *bina* without *chachma*. A man thinking who loses sight of the point of *chachma* can think no more, but his main work is the division of *bina*, because thought comes from *bina*. In speech it is the other way round: the analysis of *bina* had to be done earlier.

blocks.title: A speech at the drop of a hat
blocks.text: So a speech has to be prepared. Some people can give a speech at the drop of a hat, almost spontaneously, but it was still prepared: it is a subject they know very well, or they are the kind who go from town to town and have probably given it 25 times already. On a subject they don't know at all they could not speak. The *hisbonenus* (contemplation) has to be done ahead of time.

A person talking is not trying to divide the ideas; he already has them divided. He is trying to put them together into a coherent speech, because speech comes from *chachma*, whose work is to join the divisions into one. Yet it is *davka* the *koach hamatzref*, the power that joins, that gives strength to the *koach hamechalek*, the power that divides: without the joining there would be no real dividing.

blocks.title: Taking the gun apart
blocks.text: Even in thinking, the dividing has to work with the joining, or it is just breaking, not analysis. In the army they make you take the gun apart, so you see all the little pieces. But real analysis takes it apart with a view to how the pieces fit together: you take it apart in order to put it together, like taking a clock apart to put it together again. So they lay the pieces out in order, not all over the place: this one goes here, this one there. You break the idea up categorically, 1A, 1B, 1C.

blocks.title: The wrecking ball and the sukka
blocks.text: Taking it apart without the *metzaref* is not analysis; it is breaking, plain old *tohu* (chaos). To knock a building down you don't care which piece is which, since you won't put it back together: you take a big ball, or a bomb, and blow it up. To reconstruct it, you have to keep track of where everything is. People who build a *sukka* the first year mark the pieces when they take it apart: this is 1A, and this is 1A.

blocks.title: London Bridge, stone by stone
blocks.text: A Texan bought London Bridge, and they moved it to Austin and rebuilt it. They had to know of each stone where it fits with all the others, so they marked it: that is analysis. They could have put a bomb on it, and nobody would care how it goes back together, but that is destruction.

sensitivity.reason: A wrong fact stated as fact: London Bridge was bought by a Missouri businessman and rebuilt at Lake Havasu City, Arizona, not moved to Austin, Texas by a Texan.
sensitivity.publishable: When London Bridge was bought and moved, they rebuilt it. They had to know of each stone where it fits with all the others, so they marked it: that is analysis. They could have put a bomb on it, and nobody would care how it goes back together, but that is destruction.

blocks.text: So with the power that breaks the *nekuda* of *chachma* into subdivisions of ideas, and those into further subdivisions, down to the paragraphs, sentences, words and letters: it has to be done *davka* with a mind for the joining. That is why it is called *tziruf chilukei osios*, the joining of the divisions of letters, which sounds kind of weird. The analysis of *hisbonenus* has to be done so as to put it back together, or it is only destruction. So the text says *metzaref* where it should seemingly say *mechalek*: a divider is not enough; you need a joiner.

phrases.he: ודוקא כח העושה הצירוף הוא מבחינת מקור דבינה,
אבל גוף הצירופים בפרטי אופניהם, הרי הוא דווקא מכוון על פי הכוונה שבהשגה בפרט, על פי צמצום דמחשבת שכל העיונית
שמסדר אופן הצירופים כו' כנזכר לעיל
phrases.en: it categorizes the divisions, how they go back together again

blocks.text: *Davka* the power that makes the joining is from the source of *bina*. The body of the combinations, in their particular ways, is aimed by the intent of the particular comprehension, the contraction of analytical thought that orders them: **it categorizes the divisions, how they go back together again**. That is the whole *inyan* of analysis.

sections.title: Two mems in bina: the square makif of what one does not yet understand
sections.summary: *Bina* itself has an open *mem*, what one already thinks in and can say, and a closed *mem*, the *makif* of what one is thinking about and does not yet understand. That *makif* is square: it sits right on the head, closer at one point and farther at another, like a low ceiling.

phrases.he: ובאמת זהו בחינת מ"ם פתוחה.
כי הנה בבינה עצמה יש מ"ם סתומה ומ"ם פתוחה,
phrases.en: in the *mem stuma* of *bina* there is really the *mem psucha*

phrases.he: שנקרא מאמר סתום ומאמר פתוח
כי כל מאמר הוא במחשבה דבינה עצמה
phrases.en: *maamar* does not mean speech; it's *davka* in *machshava*

blocks.text: And really this is the open *mem*. Before, *bina* was the closed *mem* and speech the open one; now he says that **in the *mem stuma* of *bina* there is really the *mem psucha***: *bina* itself has a closed *mem* and an open *mem*, a closed saying and an open saying. For every saying is in the thought of *bina* itself. A *maamar* **does not mean speech**; it is *davka* in thought.

phrases.he: והוא ענין ההפרש בין בחינת מקיפים דאימא,
שהוא עדיין בבחינת מ"ם סתומה שמקיף מכל צד,
והוא בריבוע דוקא,
phrases.en: the *makifim* of *bina* are square

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב בזוהר על מ"ם דלםרבה המשרה כו'
phrases.en: they use a final *mem* in the middle of the word

phrases.he: ומבואר במקום אחר, ובין בחינת הארת המקיף הזה לעשות התחלקות הצירופים על ידי בחינת ה׳ גבורות מנצפ"ך כו', שהוא ענין מ"ם פתוחה מאמר פתוח
שהמחשבה הסתומה נעשית פתוחה בהתחלקות אותיות כו',
phrases.en: the *machshava stuma* becomes an open *machshava* when you can divide it into letters

phrases.he: שזהו ענין ציור המ"ם פתוחה כידוע.

blocks.text: This is the difference between the *makifim* (encompassing lights) of *Ima*, still the closed *mem* that surrounds on every side, and square, as the *Zohar* says of *lemarbe hamisra*, where **they use a final *mem* in the middle of the word**; and the shining of this *makif* that makes the division into combinations by the five *gevuros*, the open *mem*. **The *makifim* of *bina* are square**: they sit on the brain, not far away.

The *makifim* of *bina* are what you are thinking about. *Bina* has two *inyanim*: the part you understand, and the part you are thinking about, which means you don't understand it yet. That part is still only a *makif* on the *bina*, a closed *mem*. But it is not a round *makif*; it is a square one.

blocks.title: The ceiling over your head
blocks.text: A square *makif* means two things. It sits *mamash* on the brain, like an apparatus, almost within reach; a round *makif* is equidistant from the brain, which reaches it at no point and sees it from far away. And a square is not equidistant: it has corners. Look up at the ceiling: the part above you is closer than the part at the end of the room. In a room whose ceiling fit right on your head, part of it would touch your head and the rest would be farther away. So with the *makifim* of *bina*: part of what you are understanding sits right on your head, going into your brain, part is farther, and part farther still.

That is why the final *mem* is square. So *bina* has two *mems*. The open *mem*, the open saying, is what is already in your thought: you can think in it, and so you can say it. And there is the part you don't understand, which is the whole thing of *bina*. If you knew the whole thing, it would be knowledge, not *bina*; why would you be thinking about it in the first place? The part you don't know is the *makif* on your brain, and it is not totally unrelated to your brain,

or you would not think about it at all. So it is a *makif* already: you know it is there; you just don't know what it is yet. And of what you don't know, part you are almost getting, part is farther away, and part is *mamash* sitting on your brain, ready to go in.
blocks.outOfPlace: The tape was turned over mid-sentence: class 219 opens by finishing the thought class 218 broke off on, and reads line 18 again only after it.

blocks.text: The shining of this *makif* makes the division into combinations, the open *mem*. Then **the *machshava stuma* becomes an open *machshava* when you can divide it into letters**: through the division of the analysis, closed thought becomes open thought. That is the shape of the open *mem*: it has a mouth.

sections.title: The makif of bina over the middos: the mother sitting on the chicks
sections.summary: *Bina* is also a *makif* over the *middos*, like a mother sitting on her chicks: its real work is to bring down into them what is higher than its own understanding. A love that depends on a thing leaves a *makif* behind when the thing goes, and such a *makif* sits right on what it surrounds, as knowledge does.

phrases.he: וביאור הדברים,
phrases.en: now he's going to explain a little bit better

phrases.he: הנה ידוע בביאור ענין מקיפים דבינה, בענין והאם רובצת על האפרוחים כו׳
שהמדות מקבלים רק מבחינת השגה דאור פנימי דבינה
כשנקרא אם הבנים, שאז נקרא אפרוחים כו',
ובחינת גדלות המוחין דמדות בהעלם הבא מבחינת מקיפים,
היינו כשאם הבנים רובצת כו',
phrases.en: *davka* when the *bina* is sitting on top of them

phrases.he: דהיינו להמשיך מה שלמעלה מהמוחין דבינה הנמשכים למדות
phrases.en: to bring down from even higher than the *mochin* of *bina*, to bring it down into the *middos*

blocks.text: **Now he's going to explain a little bit better**, with the *makifim* of *bina* in "the mother sits on the chicks": the *middos* (emotional attributes) receive only from the comprehension of the inner light of *bina*. But now he is talking about something else. The *makifim* of *bina* are two *inyanim*: the *makif* of *bina* on itself, the part not yet understood, and *bina* as a *makif* on the *middos*.

This is already the inner light of *bina*, its open saying, but towards the *middos* it is a *makif*. *Bina* is *em habanim*, the mother, and they are the chicks. The greatness of their *mochin* comes hidden from the *makifim*, **when the *bina* is sitting on top of them**, **to bring down from even higher than the *mochin* of *bina***. The real work of *bina* is to bring down into the *middos* what is higher than itself.

phrases.he: (על דרך אהבה התלויה בדבר
שדבר זה בא באהבה בבחינת אור פנימי,
על כן כשבטל הדבר בטלה האהבה
phrases.en: when the thing goes away, the love also goes away

phrases.he: מכל מקום נשאר בבחינת מקיף,
phrases.en: still there's a *makif* of it left over

phrases.he: שהוא בחינת ההעלם מאותו הדבר,
שיוכל על ידי זה לחזור ולהתעורר ולבוא בבחינת אור פנימי כידוע)
phrases.en: so that the next time that this thing will come up, it'll be easier to love it

blocks.text: A love that depends on a thing comes as inner light, so **when the thing goes away, the love also goes away**. Still **there's a *makif* of it left over**, so when the thing comes up again it is easier to love. The second time is faster, because it was already there as a *makif*.

phrases.he: שחופף עליהם, והוא בריבוע,
phrases.en: it's over them, but it's in a square way

phrases.he: שמתיישב עליהם ממש
phrases.en: it *mamash* sits on them

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר בענין מ"ם דלמרבה כו'
וכללות הענין הוא על דרך דוגמא מידיעה במוח שמקפת את הדבר שיודע אותו, דהגם שהדבר נבדל,
מכל מקום חופף ידיעה זו ומקפת מכל צד לאותו הדבר
phrases.en: This *yedia* actually surrounds it from every place.

phrases.he: (כמו ידיעת אלהו״ת, שמשגיח ויודע את כל הנבראים,
שבידיעה זו מקיף אותם
phrases.en: this *yedia* is *makif* the thing from all sides

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב בלקוטי אמרים בידיעה שיודע כל הארץ כו')

blocks.text: The mother hovers over them, but **in a square way**: **it *mamash* sits on them**, as with the *mem* of *lemarbe*. In general it is like *yedia* (knowledge) in the mind that surrounds the thing it knows: though the thing is separate, **this *yedia* actually surrounds it from every place**. So G-d's knowledge, by which He watches over and knows all creatures, surrounds them, as in *Likkutei Amarim*: **this *yedia* is *makif* the thing from all sides**, and yet it *mamash* sits on it, not far away.

sections.title: Water and ice: the rakia over the heads of the chayos
sections.summary: An idea not yet grasped is above the limits of letters, flowing water that can still be understood many ways. Once it is grasped in one particular way it freezes into ice, the *rakia*, fixed: once it is in an explanation, that is how the explanation is.

phrases.he: וזהו כמו מה שכתוב ועל ראשי החיות רקיע כעין הקרח כו',
שהוא בחינת מקיף דבינה גם כן
(שמזה נעשה לבוש החשמ"ל מבחינת חיצוניות בינה
כמו שיתבאר)
phrases.en: this will be explained later

phrases.he: וכמו שכתוב במקום אחר בביאור ענין אור מים רקיע, דהשגה דבינה נקרא רקיע

blocks.text: This is "over the heads of the *chayos*, a *rakia* like ice": a *rakia* that *mamash* sits on their heads. It is a *makif* of *bina* too, and from it is made the *levush hachashmal*, the garment of *chashmal*, from the outside of *bina*; **this will be explained later**. And elsewhere, on "light, water, *rakia*", the comprehension of *bina* is called *rakia*.

phrases.he: לפי שקודם שבא המושכל בבחינת השגה גמורה,
phrases.en: before it comes into the actual *hasaga* of *bina*

phrases.he: עדיין הוא למעלה מבחינת הגבלת אותיות,
כמו הסבר מושכל עמוק שאינו עדיין באופן מוגבל במוח הנקרא השגה ותפיסא
הוא הנקרא מים דניידי,
phrases.en: it's called water, flowing water

phrases.he: לבא בכמה אופנים שונים כו'
phrases.en: it can come; he could really understand it in various different ways

blocks.text: Before the concept comes into full grasp it is still above the limits of letters: **before it comes into the actual *hasaga* of *bina***, it is a *makif* on the *bina*. These are the *makifim* of *bina*. A deep concept not yet limited in the mind is called *mayim d'naydi*, **flowing water**: **he could really understand it in various different ways**.

phrases.he: מה שאין כן כשבא המושכל באופן מוגבל הנתפס ומושג בכלי מוחו ממש,
phrases.en: once he understands it in a certain way and he has a certain *hasaga* into it, it is *mugbal* and *nitfas mamash* in his brain

phrases.he: נמשל לקרח, דאגלידי מיא
phrases.en: it is *nimshal* to ice: the water freezes and takes on a shape; now the water cannot flow

phrases.he: וקיימא כו'
phrases.en: and then it has to be like this

phrases.he: מלשון השג יד כו',
phrases.en: the reach of your hand

phrases.he: כמו שכתוב במקום אחר שזהו הנקרא רקיע,
phrases.en: then it's called the *rakia*

phrases.he: והוא ענין הקרח שעל גבי המוחין דחיות כו'
phrases.en: that's why it's also called *kerach*

blocks.text: But **once he understands it in a certain way**, with a certain grasp, it is limited and held *mamash* in his brain. Then **it is *nimshal* to ice: the water freezes and takes on a shape**, and can no longer flow; that is the way it is, **and then it has to be like this**. *Hasaga* is from *hasag yad*, **the reach of your hand**. So it is called *rakia*, which means fixed, and *kerach*, ice: now it is in a particular way. Once it is in an explanation, that is how the explanation is.

sections.title: The root of the ice is above bina: the chashmal, guard of the middos and source of the letters
sections.summary: The power to embody an idea in letters, an explanation or a *mashal* comes from above the inner light of *bina*, from its *makif*, the source of *bina*. That is the *levush hachashmal*, which guards the *middos* so they do not vanish when one stops thinking. It is also why an animal, which has no words, cannot feel an idea.

phrases.he: ואמנם שרש הקרח הזה שבא דוקא בבחינת הגשמה גמורה,
phrases.en: the *shoresh* of this *kerach* that comes *davka* in a way of a *hagshama gmura*

phrases.he: הוא מלמעלה מבחינת אור פנימי דבינה
phrases.en: it's really from higher than the actual *or pnimi* of *bina* itself

phrases.he: אלא הוא נמשך ונעשה מבחינת המקיף דבינה הנקרא מ"ם סתומה, שבלתי מאיר ונמשך בגלוי כלל במדות
על כן משם נעשה בחינת רקיע או קרח על גבי המוחין דמדות כו'

blocks.text: But **the *shoresh* of this *kerach* that comes *davka* in a way of a *hagshama gmura***, the complete embodiment that lets an explanation be understood, is **really from higher than the actual *or pnimi* of *bina* itself**, the *hisbonenus*. It comes from the *makif* of *bina*, the closed *mem*, which does not shine openly in the *middos*. The power to put an idea into an explanation or a *mashal* is higher than the analysis that works with its letters; it comes from the *mazalos*, from the source of *chachma*. This business runs through several chapters.

So from there comes the *rakia*, the ice over the *mochin* of the *middos*, and this is the source of the *chashmal* as well, which really comes from higher. It is the source of the letters: that ideas can be put into words, into *meshalim*, in a way of *hagshama*. That is the whole *inyan* of the last two or three chapters and the next few. It goes all the way up to the *etzem*, the source of description and definition, to *Elokim* and the *Atzmus*.

phrases.he: והיינו והאם רובצת כו',
phrases.en: the mother sits on the *middos*

phrases.he: וכן ועל גוזליו ירחף כו',
שזהו בחינת לבוש החשמ"ל שמקיף בבחינת שומר למדות
phrases.en: the *levush chashmal* that's always *makif* in a way of a *shomer* for the *middos*

phrases.he: (כמו שיתבאר בסמוך בענין כתנות עור כו',
phrases.en: the *kesones or*, the clothings

phrases.he: שמקיף לזעיר אנפין ונוקבא עד מתחת רגלי זעיר אנפין ונוקבא, שממנו נעשה המסך שבין אצילות לבריאה כו')
phrases.en: that are *makif* on the *middos* all the way to the bottom, underneath the feet of *Zu"n*, and from this *levush chashmal* becomes the *mafsik* between *Atzilus* and *Beriya*

blocks.text: This is "the mother sits" and "over his young he hovers": **the *levush chashmal* that's always *makif* in a way of a *shomer* for the *middos***, a guard. If the *middos* came only from *bina*, they would vanish the minute you stopped the *hisbonenus*. They stay because the letters they are made of, the *chashmal*, have a source higher than *bina*.

As will be explained shortly with the *kesones or*, the garments of skin, **that are *makif* on the *middos* all the way to the bottom, underneath the feet of *Zu"n*** (*Zeir Anpin* and *Nukva*): from this *levush chashmal* comes the divide between *Atzilus* and *Beriya*.

phrases.he: והוא בחינת מקור דבינה,
phrases.en: this *chashmal* really is the *makor* of *bina*

phrases.he: שמזה נמשך הכח העושה לבחינת התחלקות הצירופים דאותיות המחשבה
הנקרא מצרף,
ולא גוף הצירופים,
phrases.en: not the actual body of the separations of the letters

phrases.he: שהוא דוקא בבחינת מ"ם פתוחה מאמר פתוח כו' ודי למבין

blocks.text: This *chashmal*, which comes down to be the letters of the *middos*, **really is the *makor* of *bina***, its source. From it comes the power that divides the letters of thought, called *metzaref*, and **not the actual body of the separations of the letters**: the source of the *hagshama* and *tziyur* (form) of the idea is higher. Even the letters of the *chashmal*, *levushim* (garments) and no longer *keilim* (vessels), have a higher source.

By the way, if you look in *Shaarei Orah*, this is the problem with doing *teshuva*: a person can fix up the *middos*, the *mochin* and the *ratzon*, but the letters are still there. The letters are totally external, but their source is in the *etzem* of the soul.

So there is a closed saying. The open saying of *bina* is the actual thought in which a person thinks out the analysis; behind it is a closed saying, what he is thinking about. *V'dai lamevin*: and this is enough for one who understands.

Now we are getting into the real nitty-gritty of the whole thing: the *levush hachashmal*, the main thing needed to understand *yichuda tata'a* (the lower unity). That could be said of every chapter, but this is the main *inyan* of the *levushim*. As he said before, thought, speech and action are *Beriya, Yetzira and Asiya*, which is the *inyan* of *yichuda tata'a*.

The main thing of thought, speech and action is letters: not the inner thought of the intellect, but letters by themselves, disconnected. *Beriya, Yetzira and Asiya* are *alma d'pruda*, separate worlds. The real picture of the *Aibershter* is *davka* *yichuda tata'a*. The higher unity, what's the big deal? It is the connected world. The big *chachma* is to see His unity where it is garments and not vessels, a *davar nivdal*, a separate thing, all the way down to this world.

In chapter 44 we learned about the joinings and the divisions. The ability to put a thing into letters really comes from a joining and not a division, because the main thing is to put it together; and it comes from a higher place than the power of thinking itself.

That is the *levush hachashmal*. He saw somewhere that *chashmal* is two roots: *chash*, to feel, and *mal*, to talk. When a listener says *chash* means silence, he allows that it is also *chush*, to feel, and does not think silence is the main thing. It puts the idea in a way that it can be felt.

blocks.title: The dog that cannot ask "Why me?"
blocks.text: The mind cannot really feel an idea without putting it into words. So an animal can in a way have all the kinds of ideas we have and still not feel them, and so it has no *daas* like ours; it can never think about it philosophically, because it has no words. Dogs have problems: they worry, they cry, they are happy, they long for their people, and when their people are gone they sit there very sad; they are curious. Yet they can't put it into a *hisbonenus*. A dog is sad about certain things but never gets to think, "Why is the world like this? Why me? Is there anything I can do about it? Am I doing something wrong?" He can't put it into words, so he can't feel the idea. He has all the ideas of the emotions.

blocks.title: The rooster, the prey and the lion at the waterhole
blocks.text: An animal even has something of *bina*, as it says, "Who gives the rooster *bina* to distinguish between day and night." Animals know to go upwind or downwind of their prey, and to watch out for the lion at the waterhole: a *havchana* (discernment) of *bina*, not an emotion but something known, a *sechel*. Yet it can't progress past that. Some animals are almost as smart as a little child and still can't think like a child, though by their intelligence they should manage at least minor philosophical thoughts. They can't put the idea in a form they can grasp, hold on to and play with, because they can't put it into the letters of the *chashmal*.

And *mal* is like *milla*, a word: to say it. Without putting an idea into letters you can't say it. So *chashmal* is the power to put a concept into letters, and then you can feel it and think it over.

blocks.title: The monkey's little tools
blocks.text: That is also why animals make only small advances, like monkeys making tiny tools, and that is nothing, just trial and error: they can't think. A person can sometimes come up with a whole new idea without trying anything, just by thinking about it, because he can put it into words and play with the idea.
So the source of the *chashmal*, which is basically the *inyan* of the *levushim*, the *chashmal* of *noga* that he speaks of next, is higher than the lights themselves.

reviewQuestions.question: What is the *maamar stum* and the *maamar psuach*, and where do the sayings of "And *Elokim* said" begin?
Why does the text speak of a *metzaref*, a joining, where one would expect a power that divides? How do the gun and London Bridge show it?
Why can't a person talk while he is thinking deeply, and what has to happen before he can give a speech?
What is a square *makif*, as against a round one, and what in *bina* is it?
What are water and ice in comprehension, and why is the comprehension of *bina* called *rakia*?
Why do the *middos* not disappear when a person stops thinking, and why can't a dog ask "Why me?"

notes.text: Line 1: his reading (218 w721-749) is garbled in the transcript; the block on lines 1-3 follows the chapter's line and his rereading of its end (w750-764). "72 and 48" (w801-803), said of the 120 combinations of Elokim, and "Elokim having barkas" (w819-822) are left out as unclear.

Line 14: he remarks that the text says "metzaref" (joining) where one expects "mechalek" (dividing), and explains why it is right (218 w1438-1509, w2939-2970). That is a comment on the wording, not a correction; the text stands. The question block on it is his own question (askedBy teacher).
Lines 13-14: the long explanation of thinking and speaking (218 w1438-2970) is placed under lines 13-14, which he is explaining, though the alignment puts line 15 only at w2971.

London Bridge (218 w2690-2721): he says a Texan bought it and moved it to Austin, Texas. It was bought by Robert McCulloch and rebuilt at Lake Havasu City, Arizona. The text keeps his words; the block is flagged and its public text drops the claim.

Line 18 is read in both classes: 218 w3110 and again at the start of 219 (w80), after 219 w0-78 finishes the sentence 218 broke off on ("if it had nothing to do with your brain altogether, you..."). The 219 opening is a joined block with outOfPlace.
Line 35: the transcript has him read "bemoach" and then correct himself to "bemiddos, that's what it says here" (219 w973-996); the chapter reads "במדות".
219 w1249-1266 ("then he told her it goes all the way to the Elokim and Atzmus") is partly garbled; the block keeps only "all the way to Elokim and the Atzmus".
Line 39: in 219 he reads "שמזה נמשך כח האותיות" where the chapter has "הכח העושה" (w1509-1517); the transcript may have misheard.
"We can say that about every chapter" (219 w1762-1768) may be a listener's remark; the block gives it as a passing concession either way.

The chashmal etymology (chash, to feel; mal, to talk) he gives as something he saw someplace; a listener's "chash means silence" and his answer are one sentence in the block. The verse "Who gives the rooster bina" is from the morning blessings (Job 38:36). The Shaarei Orah reference on teshuva and the letters is as he gave it, without a place.

Phrases: many lines he reads in Hebrew without translating (lines 1, 2, 4, 5, 8, 22, 29, 35, 36, and parts of others); they have no English. Some English is his gloss right after the reading (line 3, 120 combinations; line 18, "the makifim of bina are square", said after the mem of lemarbe though it renders the earlier phrase "והוא בריבוע דוקא").
